content.title: Capital Markets, Overview - Initial Public Offering (IPO) Transaction
content.text: Initial Public Offering (IPO) Transaction Editor's Note: For an outline of major activities, responsibilities, and general timeframes for a generic, hypothetical underwritten initial public offering of common stock by a U.S. corporation, see Timeline - Initial Public Offering Transaction. The specific timing and actions required to effect an actual IPO will vary depending on the issuer, the SEC review process, and market conditions. An Initial Public Offering (“IPO”) is a company's first public offering of equity securities in which a formerly private company raises funds on a public market and becomes a public issuer registered with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC”). Before conducting an IPO, the Issuer should consider all other capital-raising options (e.g. unregistered private offerings, venture capital financing and loans). In preparations for the IPO the company may need to alter its structure, operations, financial protocols and/or corporate governance policies and procedures to comply with the ongoing reporting and other requirements of a public company that are mandated by the Securities Act of 1933 (“Securities Act”), the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Exchange Act”), the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 and the rules of the national securities exchange on which the company's securities will be listed. Offering Participants The Issuer typically hires an investment bank to serve as the lead or managing underwriter of the offering (“Underwriter”), which, in turn, assembles a syndicate of other investment banks to help market and sell the offered securities. Together, the lead underwriter and the syndicate make a commitment to purchase the securities and re-sell them to the public. Other major participants in the offering include the Issuer's outside counsel (“Issuer Counsel”), the underwriters’ outside counsel (“Underwriter Counsel”) and the Issuer's independent public accountants (“Accountants”) who ensure that the Issuer's financial statements are in compliance with securities laws and provide comfort on the financial statements in the prospectus. Regulators The IPO needs to be approved by and comply with the requirements of several regulatory bodies, including the SEC, Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (“FINRA”) and a national securities exchange on which the Issuer wants to list its securities (e.g., the New York Stock Exchange or NASDAQ). • SEC. A U.S. company may commence the registration process with the SEC by filing a Securities Act registration statement on Form S-1. As of July 10, 2017, SEC's Division of Corporation Finance is accepting voluntary draft registration statement submissions from all issuers (not just EGCs) for nonpublic review. The process for submission and for SEC's confidential review is discussed in further detail in our Overview - SEC Draft Registration Statement Review. The SEC typically responds with comments to the initial filing of Form S-1 within 30 - 40 days and the issuer must address them in a response letter and/or filed amendment to Form S-1. The issuer may go through several rounds of comments and amendments until the SEC approves the registration statement and declares it effective. Our Initial Public Offering (IPO) Timeline assumes three rounds with a two-week SEC response time for the last two rounds. • FINRA. FINRA review accompanies the SEC review and focuses on the terms of the offering and on the fairness and reasonableness of the underwriters’ compensation. FINRA typically responds with its comments within four weeks of receiving the registration statement. • Securities Exchange. Most issuers opt to list their securities on a national securities exchange to provide liquidity for their investors. To qualify for listing, the issuers must complete the listing application, pay the listing fees and meet the listing standards of their chosen exchange, all of which is typically done as part of the IPO process. Role of Due Diligence During an IPO due diligence process the Underwriters investigate the business and financials of a potential issuer to assess the risks of underwriting the offering, aid the issuer in the preparation of the offering prospectus and avail themselves of the due diligence defense under Securities Act Section 11, Section 12 and Exchange Act Rule 10b-5. The underwriters (in addition to the Issuer) have liabilities under the securities laws for incomplete, incorrect or misleading information in the offering documents. Typical Documentation The typical documentation for an IPO includes: • A Registration Statement, that discloses information about the offering and the offered securities and all relevant issuer information including, its business, management and financials; • A Prospectus, that discloses all relevant issuer information, the use of offering proceeds and any inherent risks of the investment; • An Underwriting Agreement between the issuer and the underwriters that sets forth the terms of the underwriting process; • A Transfer Agency Agreement between an issuer and a financial institution acting as a transfer agent for the securities; and • Various Legal Opinions and closing certificates. Quiet Period Several securities rules restrict communications of offering parties for a period, referred to as the “quiet period,” before the Issuer files the registration statement with the SEC through the time when the SEC declares the registration statement effective. The quiet period is generally divided into three stages: the pre-filing period, the waiting period and the post-offering period, all of which relate to the stage of SEC review of the registration statement. Different rules apply to each stage.
